rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-016 (illustrative figures), A-1: many practitioners and would-be entrants lack the degree and would not otherwise get it, so the requirement binds.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-016 (illustrative figures), A-2: the Board enforces often enough, with unenforceable contracts as a further deterrent, that many comply or stop.

No matching assumption in WE-016; judged from the text: the grandfathering clause licenses existing practitioners without the degree, and two degree programs graduate about 300 students a year, so some will hold the license.
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-016 (illustrative figures), A-3: some unlicensed practice continues undetected, mainly in homes (enforcement is complaint-driven).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-016 (illustrative figures), A-10: residential clients have close exempt or unlicensed substitutes (store design help, online services, doing it themselves).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-016 (illustrative figures), A-13: the degree and exam cover code, egress, accessibility and plan preparation, which commercial clients need to get permits approved (for homes A-14 puts the training as largely unrelated at p = 0.45, i.e. 0.55 that it is related).
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-016 (illustrative figures), A-9: license holders, schools, retailers and architects can organize at a cost below their stake.

No matching assumption in WE-016; judged from the text: the Board is funded by license fees and the general budget, and the Act gives it a new task, so the general-budget share is paid from a budget that rises with it (the handbook treats this as certain, C-27 with no assumption).
No matching assumption in WE-016; judged from the text: roughly 40% of the 6,000 people who offer interior design already hold a degree in it.
